summary: This document replaces some terminology in OSPF with wording in line with inclusive language used in the industry, following guidance from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Future OSPF documents are meant to use the new terms, even when referring to the older RFCs it updates. It changes words, not protocol behavior.

eli5.summary: Some words in an old rulebook were swapped for kinder, clearer ones. The game works exactly the same way. Only the labels changed.

questions: what is the ospf leader bit
subtitle: Swaps the master/slave wording in OSPF for Leader/Follower across seven RFCs without changing how the protocol works.

tldr.problem: OSPF specifications described the database synchronization between two routers with the terms master and slave, and named a Database Description packet bit accordingly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC replaces master/slave with Leader/Follower, renames the MS bit to the Leader (L) bit, and lists the sections of seven earlier RFCs affected. It also updates the IANA registry entry for the bit.
tldr.outcome: Only wording changes. OSPF operation and security characteristics are unchanged, and future OSPF documents are meant to use the new terms even when they reference the updated RFCs.

today: RFC 9454 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It amends RFC 2328, RFC 5340 and five other OSPF-related RFCs, and its terms are intended for all future OSPF documents.

sections.title: Why the Terms Changed
sections.content:
RFC 9454 updates some OSPF terminology to be in line with inclusive language used in the industry. The IETF designated the NIST document "Guidance for NIST Staff on Using Inclusive Language in Documentary Standards" as its inclusive language guideline.

The RFC intends that all future OSPF documents use the revised terminology, even when they reference the RFCs it updates. It updates seven documents: RFC 2328, RFC 4222, RFC 4811, RFC 5243, RFC 5340, RFC 5614 and RFC 5838.
sections.eli5: People agreed some old words should be replaced. This note lists which words change and in which books, so everyone uses the same new words from now on.

sections.title: Master/Slave Becomes Leader/Follower
sections.content:
The base OSPFv2 specification, RFC 2328, describes database synchronization as two routers forming a master/slave relationship. All instances of these terms are replaced by Leader and Follower. In the Database Description packet, the master (MS) bit becomes the Leader (L) bit.

The RFC states that the operation of OSPFv2 is not modified. The change touches the sections on synchronization of databases, the neighbor data structure, neighbor states, events causing neighbor state changes, the neighbor state machine, receiving and sending Database Description packets, an example, and the Database Description packet format in Appendix A.3.3.

OSPFv3, in RFC 5340, gets the same treatment. Its "Master/Slave (MS) bit" is renamed the Leader (L) bit, only the Database Description packet appendix is affected, and operation is again unchanged.
sections.eli5: When two routers compare notes, one used to be called the boss and one the helper. Now they are the Leader and the Follower. The way they take turns has not changed at all.

sections.title: Other Documents Touched
sections.content:
Five more RFCs get smaller edits:

  • RFC 4222, a Best Current Practice document: the "slave" in an example packet sequence in Appendix C becomes "Follower".
  • RFC 4811, Informational: in Section 2.4, "MS" for the Database Description bit becomes "L", and "Master" becomes "Leader".
  • RFC 5243, Informational: "Master or Slave" in the Introduction and all uses in the Section 3 example become Leader and Follower.
  • RFC 5614, Experimental: the neighbor state machine changes and the Section 7.5 parenthetical use the new terms and the "L" bit name.
  • RFC 5838, Standards Track: the "MS" field in a Database Description figure becomes "L".

RFC 5838 also gets one rewritten paragraph in its Section 2.4 on Hello packet processing. The new text about an interface configured for an IPv4 address family removes the non-inclusive terms pertaining to unreachability handling.
sections.eli5: Other books mention the same old words in examples and pictures. Each one gets a small list of corrections, and one paragraph is rewritten.

sections.title: IANA Registry Update
sections.content:
IANA updated the "Database Description (DD) Packet Flags" registry. The description for value 0x01 is now "Leader (L-bit)", and the references are RFC 2328 and RFC 9454.

The flag keeps the same value. Only its name and description change, which matches the RFC's statement that protocol behavior is untouched.
sections.eli5: The official list of flag names got the new label, but the flag still sits in the same slot and does the same job.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it updates terminology in OSPF RFCs without any modification to the specifications of the protocol. As a result, the security characteristics of OSPF do not change.

Implementers do not need to alter message processing, only names used in documentation, and where applicable in the registry entry.
sections.eli5: Because only the names changed, nothing about how safe OSPF is has changed either.
